There is a lot of misunderstanding about military tribunals. They are very limited in scope.

Military tribunals only try cases of treason, sedition, crimes against humanity, aiding and betting an enemy, and a couple of other types of crimes DURING TIME OF WAR. They are primarily designed to try enemy combatants who committed atrocities such as the Nuremberg Trials. Civilians can be tried as well but only if they also meet the criteria.

US citizens can be tried by military tribunal only if they too meet the criteria.

Are we at war? Well, yes and no. We having been in a declared war since WW II, but we are in several conflicts in which Congress has authorized the President to use force.

Also, a couple of the procedures for conducting military tribunals have been declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court and the Supreme Court ruled that the military tribunals eliminated too many constitutional rights. So after 9/11 the Secretary of Defense revised the procedures--some of which were still over ruled by the SC.

The last rewrite for tribunals essentially said that tribunals must use the UCMJ (Uniform Code of Military Justice) as a "guide", whatever that means, but gave no hint what had to be used and what could be ignored.

Nevertheless, tribunals have still have a couple of important differences from a court martial or a federal court. First, a tribunal doesn't have exclusionary evidence rules like courts martial and federal courts have. In other words, any evidence can be introduces regardless of how it was obtained which means classified communications intercepts and evidence seized without a warrant. And the judges in a tribunal are both the judges and the jury requiring only 2/3 of the judges to convict. There can be as few as 7 judges. 9 is more common. Last I looked, 12 were needed for a death penalty, but that may have changed.

Tribunals are normally closed and held in secret but there are exceptions such as the Nuremberg Trials. And the last major difference I can remember is that any appeals are forwarded to the Pentagon and the Secretary of Defense appoints a commission to review the convictions. Not sure what happens after that--there may be a requirement to go to the Supreme Court.

In any event, tribunals can be messy because the defense lawyers object to the procedures and it winds up in appeals courts and the Supreme Court as it has a number of times since 9/11. There is at least one tribunal at GITMO, but I've never heard of it convicting anyone. The trials were tied up for years in Federal Court arguing for the rights of the defendants and Obama let a bunch go before their trials were completed.
